doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Balancing touring, teaching and commitments
summary: Nussbaum has reduced teaching because of travel; Wall juggles two colleges and gigs and tries to be fair.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: What’s it like trying to juggle schedules? When I look at kind of what you’re doing, you’re doing some teaching, both of you seem to, and playing with all these different people. Do your commitments collide?
Well I’m not on the road like Adam.
You’re talking about the road warrior here.

I kind of cut loose my teaching for right now because I didn’t feel that I could fulfill what students should be getting. I mean when a kid is in school and they want to have a lesson every week, I wasn’t able to fulfill that. And I used to tell them up front look, I can’t see you every week, I’m going to be out for a few weeks then we can get together for two, three hours at a shot. I was realizing that that was not fair to them. Some of them said, “Oh no I still want to do it.” And you know if somebody still really wants to get together with me they can call me and I can try to do it, but I haven’t, right now, been committed to any of the schools that I was in the past. I’m still an adjunct as such. But it gets difficult. And then it gets difficult with commitments, because sometimes you’ll say to somebody yeah, I’ll do this. And somebody else you want to play with calls you and it’s like well I’m sorry but I am committed at that time. Because I’d like to be a man of my word.
Yeah. You start backing out too often—

Yeah I don’t like to do that. I mean I had the situation of sending subs in on situations and eventually they just say okay, well you’re not available, we’re going to use him. A risk you take. So right now I’m really not actively teaching. I do clinics and things like that when I’m out on the road or I’ll do some private students and things like that. And I enjoy doing them, especially when you have people who have a certain degree of ability already. Because then you can kind of help them fine tune things and it helps me fine tune things too.

But it does get tricky because this past year I’ve really gotten into a lot of college stuff that is all very enjoyable and very good but it is tricky actually doing two colleges for one thing, and then playing. Because the playing will conflict with the colleges. The colleges

will conflict with the playing. Sometimes both colleges will conflict with each other. And then I always feel bad about, it’s really all about, what I try to do is to try to keep some kind of balance. To try to be fair. To like these students here, these people are really not at the level of these people here but you still have to be fair. Is this a gig — this gig is going to conflict with that. Is this gig really that important? Maybe not. Okay, I can’t do the gig because this educational event I have to give priority to. Or vice versa. I have to go out of town and play something, okay. Have to cancel all this and then you have to reschedule and find ways of making it fair for everybody. So it’s really, it gets into a lot. There’s a way to do it. That can border on some stress at times.
Try to keep the balance. Try to keep the balance.
Trying to find the balance. That’s not easy. But it’s necessary.

Yeah. Trying to be fair and a lot of people don’t think that way. They really don’t care if they’re fair or not they just basically go for it. But if you’re dealing with students and people who you are trying — you know you’re trying to help them. You’re trying to be fair to them and to the people that are, that want you to be there, to help them.
